Maladaptive Strategies.value: I put on loud music or TV
constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette: Giovanni had always taken pride in his work as a hotel manager. He was meticulous about every detail, ensuring that guests felt welcome and comfortable during their stay. However, everything changed on that fateful day when he was exposed to toxic chemicals while inspecting the hotel's storage room. The smell of bleach and ammonia still lingered in his nostrils as he recounted the event. As he walked into the room, Giovanni noticed a strange odor, but before he could react, he felt a burning sensation in his eyes and throat. He stumbled out of the room, gasping for air, and collapsed on the floor. The next thing he remembered was waking up in the hospital, surrounded by his estranged wife and children. They told him that he had been rushed to the emergency room after being found unconscious. Giovanni couldn't shake off the feeling of helplessness that lingered long after he was discharged from the hospital. He became increasingly vigilant, always on the lookout for potential dangers lurking around every corner. Even in the comfort of his own home, he felt like an intruder could burst in at any moment. He would often find himself standing by the window, scanning the streets below, waiting for something to happen. The sound of sirens or unexpected noises made him jump, sending his heart racing. Giovanni tried to calm himself down by telling himself that it was just his imagination playing tricks on him. However, the fear lingered, and he found solace in distractions – loud music or TV – anything to drown out the constant threat monitoring that had become a part of his daily life. Giovanni's avoidance behaviors started innocently enough. He would take the long route home from work to avoid passing by the hotel where the incident occurred. However, over time, this behavior became more ingrained. He stopped attending social gatherings or meeting friends at restaurants near the hotel, fearing that he might catch a glimpse of the place and be transported back to that fateful day. His memories of the event were fragmented – disconnected pieces that didn't quite fit together. Giovanni would recall the smell of bleach, but not the face of the person who helped him out of the storage room. He remembered feeling like he was choking, but not the sound of his own voice calling for help. These disjointed recollections left him with more questions than answers. As time went on, Giovanni's distrust of his body grew. His heart would racing without warning, and he couldn't shake off the feeling that it was a harbinger of something terrible to come. He started to see his body as an enemy – constantly reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe. One day, while walking through the park, Giovanni caught a whiff of something that transported him back to the storage room. The smell of ammonia wafted up from a nearby trash can, and suddenly, he was reliving the entire ordeal – the fear, the panic, the helplessness. This time, however, there were no distractions to turn to. No loud music or TV to drown out the memories. Giovanni knew then that he needed help. As he sat in his therapist's office, Giovanni confessed that what frightened him most was losing control – of his thoughts, his emotions, and his body. He hoped that therapy could teach him how to trust himself again, how to quiet the constant threat monitoring, and how to piece together the fragmented memories that haunted him still. Giovanni looked around the therapist's office, taking in the calm atmosphere and the reassuring smile on her face. For a moment, he felt a glimmer of hope – maybe this time, he could confront his demons head-on and find some measure of peace.
